extraction.name: CoNLL-2003 named entity data
extraction.description: Language-independent named entity recognition dataset for English and German with training, development, test, and unannotated files, annotated for four entity types: persons, locations, organizations, and miscellaneous names.
extraction.creator: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder
extraction.citeAs: Erik F. Tjong Kim Sang and Fien De Meulder. Introduction to the CoNLL-2003 Shared Task: Language-Independent Named Entity Recognition. arXiv:cs/0306050v1, 2003.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was compiled from existing news corpora: English data from the Reuters Corpus and German data from the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus, specifically Frankfurter Rundschau articles. It includes annotated training, development, and test sets plus large unannotated raw data files.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data came from Reuters news stories for English and from the German newspaper Frankfurter Rundschau within the ECI Multilingual Text Corpus for German; unannotated raw data totaled 17 million English tokens and 14 million German tokens.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: English: training/development from end of August 1996, test from December 1996, raw data from September 1996. German: training/development/test from one week at the end of August 1992, raw data from September to December 1992.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Data were split into training, development, test, and unannotated files for each language; development and test were separated to avoid tuning on test data.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: All data underwent linguistic preprocessing including tokenization, POS tagging, and chunking. English used shared-task tokenizers and the memory-based MBT tagger for tagging and chunking; German used shared-task tokenizers and TreeTagger for lemmatization, tagging, and chunking.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Named entity tags for English and German training, development, and test data were created manually at the University of Antwerp, mostly following MUC conventions, with an added MISC category. The data use IOB tagging with PER, ORG, LOC, and MISC labels.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The annotation scheme assumes named entities are non-recursive and non-overlapping; when one entity is embedded in another, usually only the top-level entity is annotated.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The MISC category is very diverse, and embedded named entities are generally not annotated beyond the top level.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development/validation, testing, and semi-supervised use with unannotated data for named entity recognition systems with a machine learning component.

rai:dataCollectionTimeframe.evidence: This corpus consists of Reuters news stories between August 1996 and August 1997. For the training and development set, ten days’ worth of data were taken from the files representing the end of August 1996. For the test set, the texts were from December 1996. The preprocessed raw data covers the month of September 1996. ... All three of the training, development and test sets were taken from articles written in one week at the end of August 1992. The raw data were taken from the months of September to December 1992.

rai:dataManipulationProtocol.evidence: For each of the languages there is a training file, a development file, a test file and a large file with unannotated data. ... The split between development data and test data was chosen to avoid systems being tuned to the test data.

rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol.evidence: The participants were given access to the corpus after some linguistic preprocessing had been done: for all data, a tokenizer, part-of-speech tagger, and a chunker were applied to the raw data. We created two basic language-specific tokenizers for this shared task. The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger (Daelemans et al., 2002). The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by the decision tree tagger Treetagger (Schmid, 1995).

rai:dataAnnotationProtocol.evidence: Named entity tagging of English and German training, development, and test data, was done by hand at the University of Antwerp. Mostly, MUC conventions were followed (Chinchor et al., 1999). An extra named entity category called MISC was added to denote all names which are not already in the other categories. ... The data contains entities of four types: persons (PER), organizations (ORG), locations (LOC) and miscellaneous names (MISC). This tagging scheme is the IOB scheme originally put forward by Ramshaw and Marcus (1995).

rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis.evidence: We assume that named entities are non-recursive and non-overlapping. When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.

rai:machineAnnotationTools.evidence: The English data was tagged and chunked by the memory-based MBT tagger (Daelemans et al., 2002). The German data was lemmatized, tagged and chunked by the decision tree tagger Treetagger (Schmid, 1995).

rai:dataLimitations.evidence: An extra named entity category called MISC was added to denote all names which are not already in the other categories. This includes adjectives, like Italian , and events, like 1000 Lakes Rally , making it a very diverse category. ... When a named entity is embedded in another named entity, usually only the top level entity has been annotated.

rai:dataUseCases.evidence: For each of the languages there is a training file, a development file, a test file and a large file with unannotated data. The leaming methods were trained with the training data. The development data could be used for tuning the parameters of the leaming methods. ... When the best parameters were found, the method could be trained on the training data and tested on the test data. ... They have used the data for developing a named-entity recognition system that includes a machine leaming component.
